title: Antidistillation is Cheap: Lightweight Distillation-Resistance via Stylistic Corruption
abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a highly effective paradigm for transferring capabilities from large language models (LLMs) to smaller, more specialized student models. In commercial deployment where frontier models are restricted behind black-box APIs, sequence-level distillation remains a potent vector for competitors to clone proprietary capabilities at a fraction of the development cost. Existing defenses mostly rely on surrogate models to manipulate next-token sampling, which increases computational overhead and real-time inference latency. In this work, we propose a lightweight defense that dynamically injects style-steering vectors into the teacher model's activations upon malicious queries. This framework offers exceptional flexibility, allowing hosts to customize target defensive styles and dynamically blend them to maximize stylistic variance. Crucially, this inference-time intervention preserves semantic utility and fluency during malicious queries, misleading adversaries into believing that they are extracting pristine teacher outputs, while standard consumers continue to receive original, unmodified responses. Our experiments demonstrate that this framework successfully disrupts student learning, achieving substantial anti-distillation performance while incurring negligible overhead and preserving text naturalness. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/distill-resist-38C6/.

The framework allows hosts to customize the target defensive styles and switch among them per request, thereby making it harder for adversaries to identify a stable, learnable signature. Because this inference-time intervention largely preserves answer correctness and avoids the degenerate artifacts of prior defenses, adversaries are misled into believing they are extracting valid teacher outputs. Meanwhile, standard consumers continue to receive original, unmodified responses. Our experiments demonstrate that the framework consistently degrades student learning across model families, with minimal inference overhead. Our approach serves as a low-cost deterrent that raises the attacker's extraction and post-hoc sanitization costs. Code is available at https://github.com/anhtu96/distill-resist.

title: Probing Where Surprise Happens: Localized Violation-of-Expectation Evaluation of Video World Models
abstract: Violation-of-expectation (VOE) benchmarks evaluate intuitive physics in video world models by testing whether physically impossible events produce greater prediction errors than matched possible events. However, conventional VOE evaluations aggregate prediction errors across space and time, making it unclear whether successful discrimination reflects model's understanding of physical violations at the locations and time where they occur. To address this limitation, we introduce localized VOE evaluation, a framework that measures prediction error differences between possible and impossible events within spatial regions and temporal intervals associated with physical violations. We compare global, temporally localized, and spatiotemporally localized evaluations of V-JEPA models pretrained on developmental egocentric videos or large-scale natural video datasets. Our results reveal that global and localized judgments can diverge in both directions: global aggregation can either obscure correct localized discrimination or produce apparent discrimination without corresponding localized evidence. During continued pretraining on developmental egocentric videos, agreement between global and localized judgments changes non-monotonically, while confidence in localized judgments increases despite modest improvements in accuracy. Together, these findings establish localized VOE evaluation as a complementary diagnostic for assessing intuitive physics in video world models and demonstrate that global prediction errors do not necessarily reflect the spatiotemporal evidence of physical violations.

title: LitArc-Bench: Disentangling Text-Specific Reader-Response Dynamics from Position and Lexical Affect
abstract: When model predictions track an unfolding human affect trajectory, alignment may reflect narrative position, affective words, or text-specific reader-response dynamics. We introduce LitArc-Bench to separate these explanations: 39 Chinese-language literary excerpts segmented into seven checkpoints, with 430 questionnaires from 81 adults in two classroom groups (9,020 VAD ratings). We compare three future-blind model runs with leave-one-text-out position priors, lexical affect, and human-human references. Position alone reaches r = .470 for arousal, making raw alignment insufficient. Yet all six V/A transition advantages over a joint position-lexicon control have text-bootstrap intervals above zero. Cross-fitted models match the correct human text better than 38 mismatched texts in all nine model-dimension cells (p < .0001); a text-invariant negative control returns chance (p = 1). On human transitions at least 0.5 points against the position trend, models recover 69-76% of valence directions and 53-68% for arousal and dominance. Under crossed participant-text resampling, all nine identity intervals remain above zero; joint-control advantages are robust for valence and directional but less certain for arousal. High shape agreement still coexists with scale bias. LitArc-Bench identifies which components of literary reader response are recoverable beyond shallow explanations and why shape, calibration, and human variability require separate evaluation.

title: RL$^{\mathrm{RT}}$: On-Device Reinforcement Learning Runtime
abstract: On-device reinforcement learning runs a periodic actor and a learner on one embedded GPU shared with other workloads. Because the learner produces the actor's weights, existing designs stall the actor or let its policy drift. We present RL$^{\mathrm{RT}}$, an on-device runtime that makes this coupling a tunable parameter: a refresh bound limits actor releases between refreshes, and a GPU permit with slack-aware admission prioritises the actor and fills spare time with training atop any base scheduler. Under the real refresh cost on two Jetson boards, RL$^{\mathrm{RT}}$ keeps a 16.8 M-parameter policy's deadline misses below 1%, against 85 to 100% without it.

title: RAG-FGO: Dynamic Optimization of Query-Rewriting Agents for Generative RAG
abstract: In retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), query rewriting serves as a core interface that aligns user intent with external knowledge bases, and its effectiveness directly determines overall system performance. However, generative retrieval faces three critical challenges in real-world deployment: noisy retrieval feedback, the difficulty of jointly optimizing discrete prompt templates and continuous decoding-control parameters, and the limited generalization of static rewriting strategies under semantically complex scenarios. To address these issues, we propose RAG-FGO, a dynamic optimization framework for generative retrieval strategies. RAG-FGO formulates query rewriting as a non-differentiable black-box optimization problem in a mixed discrete-continuous space, and represents prompt templates and decoding parameters as adaptively optimizable query-rewriting agents. The framework performs global search to enable semantic jumps and structural reorganization that escape local optima, while applying local perturbations for fine-grained alignment and precise refinement. In addition, RAG-FGO introduces an elite-preserving memory pool that accumulates high-quality strategies across iterations, thereby mitigating the impact of stochasticity and noisy feedback on optimization stability. Experimental results on a diverse suite of benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed method, supporting its applicability to complex semantic retrieval tasks.

title: Bilateral Log-Linear Attention
abstract: Sequence models represent past context at different resolutions, using token-level keys and values, fixed-size recurrent states, or hierarchies of compressed summaries. Full attention supports strong associative recall but requires quadratic work during training and prefill and a linearly growing key-value cache during inference. Linear attention and state-space models reduce these costs through fixed-size recurrent memory, but this compression can limit recall. Log-linear attention offers a middle ground by maintaining logarithmically many state matrices. However, its hierarchy favors finer resolution near the current query while compressing earlier context into coarser summaries. To complement this allocation of resolution, we introduce bilateral log-linear attention, which pairs the existing hierarchy with a second hierarchy anchored at the sequence origin. By combining their reads, the two branches provide finer access to both early and recent context while remaining causal. We derive recurrent and chunkwise parallel formulations for the added branch, preserving log-linear training and prefill work, logarithmic decoding work per token, and logarithmic persistent state storage at fixed feature dimensions and chunk size. In multi-query associative recall, this design raises mean overall test accuracy from 76.37% to 96.12% over forward log-linear attention across multiple training seeds. For pretrained language models under approximate parameter matching, it raises the mean score on six selected RULER needle-in-a-haystack tasks from 26.97% to 50.03% at a context length of 6144 tokens. In the same setting, bilateral attention also outperforms forward log-linear attention on seven of eight downstream retrieval tasks, including question answering and information extraction.

title: Fuse-PINN: Combining Finite Element Methods and Physics-Informed Neural Networks to enable massively parallel simulations of non-linear PDEs
abstract: Research in the domain of Physics-Informed Neural Networks applied to PDE modelling has advanced significantly in recent years, providing a wide ecosystem of novel methods. However, one frequent limitation is the inability of PINNs to scale out on High-Performance Computing architectures to address more ambitious challenges, particularly non-linear physics models with turbulent dynamics in large spatial domains. Typical studies restrain demonstrations to toy models with simple physics equations, few variables, and rarely any complex non-linear dynamics evolved over long timescales. Part of the AI community has even adopted the idea that "PINNs don't scale". This work proves otherwise. We present a mathematically robust formulation of Finite-Element-Method for Neural Networks (FEM-NN) implemented into a comprehensive, modular framework: Fuse-PINN. This formulation provides the basis for a sclable parallelisation of Physics-Informed Neural Networks on GPU-based HPC systems. Furthermore, an Energy Natural Gradient Descent optimiser is implemented to allow high-precision convergence. Fuse-PINN is demonstrated on physics models relevant to Magnetic Confinement Fusion, including non-linear convective models with fine-scale dynamics. Near-perfect scaling is achieved on multi-GPU runs with increasing problem size.

title: Multi-level latent-diffusion adaptation for cross-region point cloud segmentation of ancient terraces
abstract: Automated lidar feature detection from lidar point clouds can support archaeological surveys, but models trained in one landscape may transfer poorly to another because of differences in terrain, vegetation, acquisition characteristics, and feature morphology. We address this problem for cross-region detection of ancient terraces using transductive unsupervised domain adaptation that exploits an unlabelled target survey. We propose MELD (Multi-level Embedding-space Latent Diffusion), which trains separate diffusion denoisers on target-domain representations at four hierarchical PointNet++ feature levels. These target distribution priors are then used to refine source representations during supervised training and target representations during inference, allowing adaptation to act directly on the multi-scale features consumed by the segmentation decoder. We additionally investigate local geometric descriptors derived from K-nearest-neighbour neighbourhoods, including surface normals, slope, and aspect. MELD is evaluated bidirectionally between the Teyuna and Miraflores lidar surveys in the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, Colombia, against a source-only model and nine configurations of established domain adaptation approaches. MELD raises F1 over the source-only model from 0.397 to 0.459 for Teyuna-to-Miraflores transfer and from 0.557 to 0.594 in the reverse direction, achieving the highest F1 among the evaluated adaptation methods in both directions. Adding local geometry further raises F1 to 0.542 and 0.606, respectively. Multi-level ablation shows that refining all four PointNet++ levels provides the strongest performance in both directions. These results show that explicit modelling of target feature distributions in hierarchical point cloud feature space, complemented by local geometry, provides an effective route to cross-region archaeological mapping without target labels.

title: Towards Seconds-level Video Representation: Quadratically Gated Feature Grid with Adaptive, Prediction-free Sampling
abstract: Implicit neural video representations are notoriously slow to build, which does not cross the basic practical threshold for most industrial applications. Here, we present Q-GAS, a coordinate-queryable video representation that couples multi-resolution explicit 3D feature grids with a compact SwiGLU-style quadratic-gating (QG) decoder and an error-aware, prediction-free sampler. The explicit grids avoid hash-collision coefficient sharing at the cost of modestly higher storage yet greatly boost the expressive capacity; the QG decoder introduces low-rank local second-order interactions to improve the nonlinear feature response. During fitting, a global error map periodically refreshes a high-error pool, and each batch mixes pool samples with uniform samples, which is free from the auxiliary model to predict difficult samples, thereby further escalating the efficiency. On UVG Beauty/Bosphorus/Jockey, Q-GAS fits and quantizes under 50 s on one RTX PRO 6000, decodes at over 370 FPS with mixed precision and about 146 FPS in FP32. In our PyTorch implementation, Q-GAS trains and quantizes 5.5-7.2 times faster than the evaluated Instant-NGP baseline and 19-28 times faster than RNeRV. Under a 90 s budget, it improves PSNR/MS-SSIM/LPIPS over the evaluated NeRV-family pipelines at comparable BPP over the measured overlap. We have shared our code at https://github.com/MillenRosen/Q-GAS for readers' free use.

title: Backpropagation-Free Continual Learning: A Unified Energy-Based Framework, Reproducible Benchmark, and Open Challenges
abstract: Backpropagation has been the dominant credit-assignment mechanism behind the deep-learning revolution, yet it is global, memory-hungry, biologically implausible, and costly on hardware dominated by data movement. In parallel, predictive coding, equilibrium propagation, contrastive Hebbian learning and forward-only schemes have shown that useful credit assignment can also arise from local variables and the relaxation of an energy function. This manuscript is a review with a reproducible benchmark, not a proposal of a new learning rule. We organise existing backpropagation-free methods and continual-learning strategies under a common Local Equilibrium Learning (LEL) formulation, re-validate the core theoretical links numerically, and use a controlled continual-learning benchmark as an auditable case study within the review. The theoretical contribution is unification and verification, not priority over predictive coding, equilibrium propagation or replay. The empirical contribution is diagnostic rather than exhaustive: a benchmark of catastrophic forgetting with local networks that makes the review reproducible. We compare regularisation (EWC, SI), noise replay and generative “dreaming” across MNIST, Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10 in two independent implementations. Generative replay with local generators turns class-incremental Split-MNIST forgetting (chance level, the same as EWC and SI) into 86.8±0.2%, which is 96% of the joint-training ceiling and 97.4% in the task-incremental setting; the same mechanism reaches 82.0% on Fashion-MNIST and 37.0% on CIFAR-10. A matched control that holds the retention mechanism fixed and swaps only the learning rule shows that backpropagation with the same generative replay reaches a comparable or slightly higher accuracy than LEL (90.3% vs. 86.7% class-incremental); the benefit is attributable to generative replay as a retention mechanism, not to the local learning rule itself, which we state plainly rather than let the headline number imply otherwise. The CIFAR-10 number is intentionally reported as a limitation of a shallow raw-pixel local model, not as a claim of competitiveness with modern CNNs or transformers trained by backpropagation. We separate positive results; negative results and open limitations; and release scripts, seeds, dataset preparation and configuration files so that this paper can serve as an honest entry point for backpropagation-free continual learning.

title: Three Invisible Failure Modes in Speech-Based Age Estimation for Child Safety
abstract: Child safety in AI depends on the accurate identification of minor users. Young children tend to talk rather than type when interacting with AI, so in practice this identification requires predicting age from speech. We evaluated whether three audio-capable large language models can predict a child's age from their speech across five studies using two speech corpora of children under the age of 13. Models classified children as over 13 on 2.5% to 42.5% of audio responses, and every model that answered placed some 5- to 11-year-olds over 18. While measuring these rates, we uncovered three distinct failure modes. A client library silently double-encoded speech samples, leading one model to classify children aged 5 to 10 years old as being in their thirties and forties with hallucinated explanations. A second model's endpoint was replaced by a successor that refused nearly every age-related question and never produced an age. Every model sometimes placed the same speech sample under 13 and over 18 years of age, but a third model went further, giving threshold answers that contradicted its own numeric estimates. None of these failure modes produced a warning, a status code, or a change in output format, so they would all pass standard monitoring. These results demonstrate why child-safety claims about age assurance should be evaluated at the level of the pipeline rather than the model. We describe the reporting practices that would make such failures detectable.

title: PerfArena: Ranking LLMs by Code Performance
abstract: Industry now relies on LLMs to write a large share of production code. Although that code is mostly, but not always, correct, correctness alone does not determine whether it is fit for repeated and extensive use, which depends on what the code costs in time, memory and energy. Most code-generation benchmarks nonetheless evaluate correctness in isolation, and most performance-oriented benchmarks cover few languages and rarely measure energy consumption. To address this gap, we present PERFARENA, an open-source, reproducible arena that ranks LLMs by the performance of their generated code across multiple languages and competitions. PERFARENA executes the solutions of each LLM on a Unix-like host and reports correctness together with latency, peak memory, and energy consumption. Correctness oracles, performance oracles, profilers, and code-generation workflows are pluggable in PERFARENA, enabling the integration of new judging backends and measurement tools without changing the pipeline. We evaluate PERFARENA on two competitions: CLBGComp, 10 compute-intensive benchmarks from the Computer Language Benchmarks Game, and LeetCodeComp, 99 LeetCode problems whose accepted solutions differ measurably in latency. Currently, PERFARENA holds 9,455 correct and measured solutions from 13 state-of-the-art LLMs across 7 programming languages. Across both competitions, got-6-astra is the only LLM that no other LLM beats significantly in latency, energy consumption, or peak memory, solving 99.7% of LeetCodeComp and 100% of CLBGComp. All PERFARENA leaderboards and measured solutions are publicly available, providing a continuously updated reference that helps developers choose an LLM per language and metric, instead of relying only on correctness rates or pricing.

title: Direction or Magnitude? Learning Scalars over Task-Calibrated Directions
abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) aims to preserve adaptation quality while reducing training costs. We propose SCALAR, which achieves performance comparable to LoRA with substantially fewer trainable parameters, lower peak training memory, and higher throughput. SCALAR constructs a fixed input basis from task activations and assigns a random output dictionary to each input direction. Fine-tuning learns only layer-specific scalar coefficients, reducing gradient and optimizer-state storage. Grouped computation aggregates output atoms before applying the adapter to token activations, while dictionary sharing across compatible layers reduces fixed-basis storage. Experiments on commonsense reasoning, mathematical reasoning, code generation, and knowledge evaluation after instruction tuning demonstrate effective adaptation at small trainable budgets. On commonsense reasoning, SCALAR achieves accuracy comparable to LoRA with about 4% of its trainable parameters. System measurements on Qwen2.5-7B show 20% lower peak training memory and 6% higher throughput than LoRA. evidence.abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) aims to preserve adaptation quality while reducing training costs. We propose SCALAR, which achieves performance comparable to LoRA with substantially fewer trainable parameters, lower peak training memory, and higher throughput. SCALAR constructs a fixed input basis from task activations and assigns a random output dictionary to each input direction. Fine-tuning learns only layer-specific scalar coefficients, reducing gradient and optimizer-state storage. Grouped computation aggregates output atoms before applying the adapter to token activations, while dictionary sharing across compatible layers reduces fixed-basis storage. Experiments on commonsense reasoning, mathematical reasoning, code generation, and knowledge evaluation after instruction tuning demonstrate effective adaptation at small trainable budgets. title: Contextual Non-Convex Bandit Optimization with Two-Point Feedback
abstract: We study a non-stochastic contextual bandit problem with Lipschitz losses. At every round, the learner observes the context then picks two actions, observes the difference between their losses, and incurs their mean. The aim is to minimize the regret against a generic non-parametric comparator class of policies mapping contexts to actions; for example, Lipschitz policies and Hölder-smooth policies. We show how relying on a hierarchical discretization technique allows us to improve upon the regret rates achievable under one-point feedback, and even recover the full-information rate in some cases; notably, for sufficiently smooth policy classes or low-dimensional instances. Additionally, for Lipschitz policies, we present an algorithm whose per-round computational complexity is only logarithmic in the time horizon.

title: Deep Neural Networks Training Efficiency: Does Grokking Modify its Dynamics?
abstract: We study whether grokking, the delayed emergence of out-of-distribution generalization after apparent overfitting, alters training efficiency in deep neural networks, where efficiency is measured as accuracy per unit energy. Using two canonical settings, modular arithmetic and MNIST, we analyze two neural network models under 16-, 32-, and 64-bit precision and use Orthograd to test whether grokking produces noticeable deviations from the typically decreasing dynamics of training efficiency. We consider both short training runs of up to 500 epochs and long training runs of up to 20,000 epochs, and in both cases identify grokking as a sharp improvement in test accuracy after a sustained train-test gap. In the short-horizon experiments, applying Orthograd at progressively stronger levels during early training does not induce grokking, and efficiency remains smoothly decreasing. In the long-horizon experiments, Orthograd induces grokking, but the efficiency curves remain approximately monotonic and show no appreciable local increase at the grokking transition. These results suggest that, in our setting, grokking does not materially alter overall training-efficiency dynamics.

title: Beyond Bot Labels: Retrospective Consequence-Grounded Ranking of Attributed Cache Harm in E-Commerce Logs
abstract: Web caches reduce origin load and latency, but automated traffic can either warm them or evict objects shoppers reuse, lowering the cache hit ratio (CHR). Existing bot defenses generally infer automation from User-Agent (UA) strings or behavior rather than identify sessions that impose cross-session cache harm. We instead formulate the task as ranking sessions by eviction damage and propose consequence-grounded session ranking. A single chronological replay attributes each eviction-induced miss by a protected shopping session (a victim) to the session whose insertion last evicted the object. A behavioral model predicts the target from session behavior alone. Selected sessions bypass the cache but remain origin-served. In a controlled check of 539 non-victim sessions selected across harm levels, attribution order tracks victim-hit changes after removal (Spearman correlation 0.80). On a 12.7-million-request real trace, the top 1% of sessions carry 48.8% of attributed harm. Sessions without bot tags contribute 49.1% of this tier's harm. At the 20% request-volume target, the default conditional CHR difference reaches 93% of the UA baseline, which selects 47 times as many sessions. Six training seeds show little variation. This comparison conditions on the victims that remain, so we also report victim bypass. Local replay and retraining on a second store reproduce harm concentration and a top tier dominated by sessions without bot tags. These results establish attributed cross-session harm as an outcome-based target for retrospective cache audits and selective intervention design.

title: TReC: Evaluating Move-Induced State Changes in Instruction-Conditioned Go
abstract: When a Go model predicts a move different from the expert's, coordinate distance measures how far the prediction lands from the reference. We introduce Transition Representation Consistency (TReC) to compare how the two moves change a board-state embedding. Both moves are executed from the same position under the game rules, and TReC is the cosine similarity between the two resulting representation changes. In experiments with a frozen KataGo network on 680 mid-to-late-game positions from five games, the gap between the highest and lowest candidate per position has a median of 0.01 to 0.08 for the direct successor-state cosine and 0.88 to 1.33 for TReC, depending on the evaluator layer. TReC follows coordinate distance only weakly: the rank correlation between a candidate's distance to the reference and its TReC, computed within each position, has a median of -0.19 over these positions.

title: Characterizing the blast radius of triple level poisoning attacks in knowledge graph retrieval augmented generation systems
abstract: KG-RAG (Knowledge Graph RAG) systems link entities by typed relational edges and support multi-hop reasoning chains in which one corrupted fact can spread across many inference paths at once. In this paper, we formally define and quantitatively assess the blast radius (corrupted queries per injected triple) of three triple-level poisoning strategies on Knowledge Graph RAG: edge poisoning, hub poisoning, and chain poisoning. Experiments on a biomedical knowledge graph built with Microsoft GraphRAG v0.3.6 and Gemma 2 9B show hub poisoning reaches a blast radius of $$14.0\times $$ , against $$7.0\times $$ for edge poisoning and $$4.0\times $$ per triple for chain poisoning, from a $$0\%$$ pre-poisoning baseline. Two-hop queries show the steadiest effect, and cascade corruption exceeds direct impact in every condition. We implement a graph-aware defense based on a degree-weighted trust score that uses entity centrality as a proxy for injection risk. At the reported operating point the filter queues the hub injection and $$4.1\%$$ of baseline triples, and does not queue the edge or chain injections.

title: Context Matters: Improving LLM-Based Code Summarization with Hierarchical Information
abstract: Source code documentation plays an important role in software quality activities, such as code review, program comprehension, maintenance, and bug fixing. However, it is often fragmented across individual code elements and focuses on local implementation details, providing little information about their surrounding context. This limits both developers' understanding of software systems and the effectiveness of Large Language Models (LLMs), whose reasoning is constrained by finite context windows. Enriching documentation with hierarchical context has the potential to improve software comprehension and support downstream, quality-related tasks for both developers and LLM-based tools. In this paper, we present an in silico study that showcases the impact of augmenting context on the generation of code-level documentation, using a variety of LLMs. By varying the function, class, and module hierarchy visible to the LLMs, we assess whether this variation produces a significant difference in the resulting code documentation compared with the existing documentation, which serves as a proxy for developer intent. Our results show that Documentation-Aware prompts with class or module-level context consistently yield summaries that are closest to the original documentation. Adding surrounding documentation yields statistically significant improvements over the baseline across models, with effect sizes ranging from negligible (DeepSeek) through weak (GPT-4o-mini) to medium (Gemini). We restrict the study to this immediate hierarchical context; call-graph traversal and cross-module dependency context fall outside our scope and are left to future work. These findings provide a clear path to improve automated documentation tools and enhance LLMs' ability to reason about codebases for downstream tasks, such as code retrieval.

title: Smart Home Agents Make Capable but Unpredictable Grid Operators
abstract: AI-enabled smart homes are becoming more common across the grid edge. However, there has not been much work on failure response. This area is critical because smart homes operate on the grid edge where failures can cascade down. If a power outage happens within a smart home, a user has to manually troubleshoot their smart home to include tasks such as power load balance and device recovery. We conduct the first resilience analysis of smart home agents across a full power outage, providing a suite of outage simulations in a live environment that measures resilience before, during, and post power outage. We show that smart home agents can act as grid operators in power outages and identify several new failure categories highlighting the current limitations across all of our models. These findings establish the groundwork for smart home agents as grid operators to increase overall resilience on the grid edge.

title: A Generalizable Approach to Safety-Aware Robotic Behavior Planning with an Explicit Constraint Space
abstract: Large language and vision-language models have substantially advanced robotic behavior planning from natural-language instructions and visual observations. However, safe manipulation in tabletop environments remains challenging because the safety constraints required for a task depend on the surrounding scene and may not be explicitly specified in the instruction. We propose a safety-aware behavior planning framework based on an explicit Constraint Space that stores reusable textual safety rules. Rather than retrieving rules solely by semantic similarity, we formulate constraint selection as task- and environment-conditioned applicability learning. A lightweight query-conditioned dual-tower model identifies the constraints applicable to the current context, which are then provided together with the original task and image to a multimodal behavior planner. To handle incorrect constraint selections and previously unseen hazards, we introduce a multimodal Safety Inspector that evaluates generated primitive plans, reconstructs the complete applicable constraint set, and provides corrective planning feedback. Validated inspection feedback is further used for test-time adaptation of constraint applicability and parameter-efficient adaptation of the Safety Inspector through LoRA, while newly identified constraints are incorporated into the Constraint Space. The resulting framework integrates explicit safety knowledge representation,context-aware constraint selection, corrective safety inspection, and test-time knowledge adaptation for safety-aware robotic behavior planning.

title: SpecRelay: Amortize or Avoid the Round Trip in Edge-Cloud Speculative Decoding
abstract: Edge-cloud speculative decoding moves autoregressive drafting to an edge device while a larger cloud model verifies draft tokens in parallel, so that edge drafting and cloud verification overlap under a synchronous draft-verify schedule. Beyond low-latency local networks, however, the next verification request of that schedule can be sent only after the previous reply arrives, so every round still waits out a full round trip, and throughput falls as the network RTT grows. To recover this loss, we present SpecRelay, an edge-cloud LLM inference system that addresses this cost at two levels: it amortizes round trips when cloud verification is necessary and avoids them when local reasoning suffices. For cloud-bound queries, an asynchronous verification pipeline keeps fixed-budget draft trees in flight while earlier replies are still outstanding, and the cloud rejects stale requests before the target-model forward pass (the asynchronous schedule). At the query level, an RTT-conditioned router (the Latency-Aware Router) estimates quality and completion latency for three on-device modes (direct generation, Chain-of-Draft, and full reasoning) and cloud speculative decoding, selecting among them under a configurable accuracy-latency objective without adding latency during inference, since the router runs concurrently with the draft-model prefill. The asynchronous schedule alone improves decoding throughput by up to 50% over a reproduced synchronous baseline across multiple benchmarks. At matched target-model accuracy and 250 ms of added round-trip latency, the full system with the router delivers 1.95x and 1.55x the throughput of the same baseline on SPROUT and OlympiadBench, respectively, while sending only 47% and 39% of the queries to the cloud.

title: Lipschitz-Constrained Discriminators in Generative Modeling: Asymptotic Behavior and Support Mismatch
abstract: We study the asymptotic behavior of optimal discriminators associated to $L-$Lipschitz regularized KL-divergences of two probability distributions $Q$ and $P$ that interpolate between the rescaled Wasserstein$-1$ metric by some parameter $L>0$ and the KL divergence. The parameter $L$ plays the role of a Lipschitz constraint and is viewed as a regularization parameter: small values of $L$ enforce a more geometry-aware discriminator, while as $L$ increases the geometric regularization is progressively relaxed. It is a known result [3] that such divergences converge to the KL divergence as $L\to\infty$. In this paper, we characterize the asymptotic behavior of the optimal discriminators as $L\to\infty$ in different regimes: Firstly, under $Q\ll P$ and the Radon-Nikodym derivative $\frac{dQ}{dP}$ is bounded from above and bounded away from zero. Secondly, when $Q$ and $P$ are discrete distributions satisfying $Q\ll P$, and finally when $Q$ and $P$ are non absolutely continuous discrete distributions. This result motivates training strategies which involve discriminators, such as adversarial generative models. In practice, the data distribution is often represented by a discrete empirical measure, while, especially at the early stages of the training, the model distribution may have little or no overlap with the empirical data distribution.

title: JaRS: Contrast-Free Localization of Memorized Regions in Diffusion Models via Jacobian Row Sums
abstract: Diffusion models sometimes memorize and reproduce regions of their training images, raising privacy and copyright concerns. We aim to localize these regions. Existing contrast-based methods use the diagonal of the denoiser Jacobian, which reflects the posterior variance of each pixel. However, a small diagonal entry is ambiguous: it signals either memorization or averaging over many neighboring pixels in smooth or predictable regions. To resolve this ambiguity, these methods subtract a reference map, which requires a second evaluation with a null prompt or an earlier checkpoint. Unconditional models have no null prompt, and earlier checkpoints are unavailable in general. We show that Jacobian row sums (JaRS), unlike the diagonal, separate memorization from local averaging without a reference map. Pairing JaRS with an image-level detection score that uses the same statistic at an early denoising step yields JaRS+. Across Stable Diffusion v1.4 and v2.1, Realistic Vision v5.1, and an unconditional diffusion Transformer (DiT), JaRS+ outperforms contrast-based localization methods.

title: Certified Improvements to Best-Known Thomson-Problem Configurations with a Search Pipeline Built with Large Language Model Agents
abstract: The Thomson problem asks for N unit charges on a sphere with minimum Coulomb energy; for large N the best configurations known are curated in the Cambridge Cluster Database, whose largest-N entries were set in October 2026. We report configurations for N = 912, 1382 and 2502 with energies 0.0036186, 0.0109730 and 0.0614033 below the database values, certified by exact integer arithmetic. All three are numerically strict local minima modulo rotations and keep the defect inventory and scar compositions of the database configurations; the database value for N = 912 had been reached by two different methods. Our search runs unconstrained replica-exchange basin hopping from the database configurations, with a shared pool of minima, recombination of improved regions after relabelling by geometry, and gradient-only polishing; replica-exchange basin hopping alone found the N = 912 and 1382 configurations, the former in one of five runs. We built and ran it with large language model agents (Claude, through a chat interface and the Claude Code agent), and we report every search, including those that failed. Two findings matter for others who search the database. Polishing alone lowers two entries by more than the threshold at which our pipeline reports a candidate, which produced two spurious records until candidates were compared with the polished database energies (the polished baseline). A local-relaxation speed-up passed its exactness test yet found nothing in a controlled comparison in which every arm with full relaxation went below the database value within 15 minutes. We distil three practices for computational discovery with large language model agents: calibrate the search code and verify candidates with code separate from the search, compare candidates with the polished baseline, and test design changes in controlled comparisons with pass criteria fixed in advance.

title: Accelerating Atomistic-Continuum Simulations of Multilayer 2D Materials with Functional Principal Component Analysis-Based Machine Learning
abstract: Atomistic-continuum simulations of complex wrinkling deformations in large-area multilayer two-dimensional (2D) materials are computationally expensive. To accelerate these simulations, this work presents a machine-learning (ML) framework that first constructs a low-dimensional representation of the deformation field, then learns the deformation in this reduced space. Dimensionality reduction of deformed 2D membranes is challenging because of the extremely high dimensionality of discretized deformation fields, the need to preserve surface continuity and prescribed geometric constraints, the stochastic nature of wrinkling patterns, and the limited availability of training data. We address these challenges using two-dimensional functional principal component analysis (FPCA). The proposed FPCA representation reduces deformation fields containing millions of degrees of freedom to latent spaces with only tens of dimensions while preserving the continuity of the deformed surface. In addition, prescribed homogeneous boundary constraints are satisfied exactly through an appropriate choice of basis functions in the FPCA representation. A neural network is then trained to predict the principal components from the system and loading parameters. The resulting ML-predicted deformation fields are used as high-quality initial configurations for the atomistic-continuum solver, which subsequently performs energy minimization to obtain equilibrium solutions. The framework is demonstrated for multilayer graphene subjected to uniaxial compression, biaxial compression, and combined biaxial compression and simple shear. For the most computationally intensive large-strain cases, the proposed approach achieves speedups of at least 6.8 times while converging to final energies comparable to, and in some cases lower than, those obtained using conventional atomistic-continuum initialization.

Dimensionality reduction of deformed 2D membranes is challenging because of the extremely high dimensionality of discretized deformation fields, the need to preserve surface continuity and prescribed geometric constraints, the stochastic nature of wrinkling patterns, and the limited availability of training data. We address these challenges using two-dimensional functional principal component analysis (FPCA). The proposed FPCA representation reduces deformation fields containing millions of degrees of freedom to latent spaces with only tens of dimensions while preserving the continuity of the deformed surface. In addition, prescribed homogeneous boundary constraints are satisfied exactly through an appropriate choice of basis functions in the FPCA representation. A neural network is then trained to predict the principal components from the system and loading parameters. The resulting ML-predicted deformation fields are used as high-quality initial configurations for the atomistic-continuum solver, which subsequently performs energy minimization to obtain equilibrium solutions. The framework is demonstrated for multilayer graphene subjected to uniaxial compression, biaxial compression, and combined biaxial compression and simple shear. For the most computationally intensive large-strain cases, the proposed approach achieves speedups of at least 6.8 times while converging to final energies comparable to, and in some cases lower than, those obtained using conventional atomistic-continuum initialization.

title: WeatherDreamer: Learning a World Model from Multimodal Earth Observations
abstract: Machine learning weather models now rival operational global forecasts but still start from analyses produced by separate, expensive data assimilation (DA) systems, which for global models are typically updated every six hours. Observation-to-observation models avoid this dependence, but most omit the recursive filtering cycle that lets DA systems carry a background state through sparse, irregular observations. We introduce WeatherDreamer, a world model that learns this cycle end-to-end from 18 global observing systems, without reanalysis. It infers a latent state from observations, carries it forward hour by hour with learned dynamics, corrects it each hour with new observations, and can predict what any of its observing systems would measure at any location. At held-out stations, its ensembles beat NOAA's Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS) for temperature, dew point and wind out to 12 h and are better calibrated than GEFS and the ECMWF ensemble. Precipitation, cloud-top height and solar irradiance, never inputs at inference, are inferred with skill matching or exceeding operational products at short leads. Against the first guess of NOAA's Gridpoint Statistical Interpolation (GSI) DA system, WeatherDreamer's short-range departures are within 10% of GSI's at surface stations and within 25% for moisture-sensitive microwave channels, but up to five times larger for temperature-sounding channels. Never given observation errors, its learned update assumes errors close to known instrument and retrieval errors of microwave sounders and scatterometer winds. WeatherDreamer also separates viewing geometry from atmospheric state, recovering 83-96% of observed limb darkening and producing seamless nadir-view imagery. Producing an hourly global analysis in about 1.5 minutes on one GPU, WeatherDreamer shows that assimilation and forecasting can be learned together directly from observations.

title: Vision-Language-Action Models: A Life-Cycle Survey of Design, Training and Deployment
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models adapt web-pretrained vision-language models to output robot actions, so that web knowledge carries over to physical control. In under 4 years the field has moved from RT-2, the first VLA, to open models that fine-tune on a single consumer GPU and to proprietary generalists that clean unseen homes. This survey reviews 88 works from December 2022 to October 2026, mainly on manipulation and navigation, plus humanoid control, world-action models and evaluation. We follow a VLA through its life cycle, from model design to training and deployment, along seven axes. Model design covers (a) inputs and memory, what the model observes; (b) architecture, how its pipeline is built; (c) action output, how it produces motor commands; and (d) intermediate predictions, what else it predicts, from reasoning steps to future observations. Training covers (e) pretraining data, the mix of robot, web, human and simulated data, and (f) post-training, adaptation to the target robot. Deployment covers (g) real-time execution, keeping pace with the robot. We analyse 22 models on these axes and report their training data, model size, inference speed and hardware. Three trends emerge: (i) training data has broadened, from about 10,000 hours of teleoperated robot data ($π_0$) to 23,000 community-collected episodes (SmolVLA) and 20,000 hours of egocentric human video (GR00T N1.7); (ii) model sizes have split: most recent models have 3-7 billion parameters, while a new group under one billion runs on consumer GPUs; and (iii) generalist VLAs are emerging that handle both manipulation and navigation, such as UniVLA and Qwen-VLA. We also compare VLAs with world-action models, which predict future observations as well as actions. We review evidence that some VLAs with near-perfect benchmark scores fail when objects or the camera move slightly, and open up further research questions.

title: RSSA: Robust Semantic and Spatial Aligner for Collaborative Perception
abstract: V2X collaborative perception improves single-vehicle perception by aggregating multi-view features from collaborative agents. However, existing methods typically rely on simple spatial warping to align the collaborative features, which can cause semantic misalignment during fusion. Meanwhile, these deterministic warping-based methods are highly sensitive to the positional noises. In this paper, we propose a plug-in module called Robust Semantic and Spatial Aligner (RSSA), which performs semantic and probabilistic spatial transformations for robust feature alignment. Specifically, a Semantic Transformation (SemT) block modulates feature channels based on the observed relative pose to correct semantic inconsistencies. Subsequently, a Probabilistic Spatial Transformation (P-SpaT) block performs probabilistic warping by sampling from the Gaussian-modeled relative pose space. A Relative Transformation Augmentation (RT-Aug) strategy is further introduced to augment the relative poses and facilitate the training of the RSSA. Extensive experiments on both simulated and real-world datasets demonstrate that RSSA improves the state-of-the-art methods by a large margin under the configuration of both clean and noisy positions.

title: Beyond Prediction Gain: LASR as a Metric for Action-Grounded Latents in World Models
abstract: World models that support planning, control, and interpretable reasoning require latent representations that genuinely encode action. Yet the large-scale video data from which such models are learned overwhelmingly lack action annotations. Latent-action models infer action-like variables from observation sequences, enabling action-aware learning from unlabeled videos or trajectories. A fundamental concern, however, remains: a latent that improves future prediction may simply encode the current state, episode progress, task identity, or other predictive shortcuts. Existing evaluation practices---reconstruction loss, rollout fidelity, action recovery, or downstream performance---cannot isolate this distinction. We introduce the Latent Action Support Ratio (LASR), a dimensionless metric that measures, under offline evaluation on held-out data, whether a learned latent provides predictive support for action-related targets beyond the current state and non-action alternatives. LASR provides two complementary summaries: GeoLASR captures typical support, while WorstLASR identifies the weakest case. We instantiate the LASR benchmark with recorded actions and corresponding physical state changes as targets, episode-held-out splits, one predictor type for all comparisons, and positive and negative controls. Experiments on recorded robot manipulation data and a matched multi-task panel demonstrate that LASR detects known action information, rejects representative non-action shortcuts, and enables graded comparisons among imperfect latent representations. We further use LASR to train and audit a lightweight residual adapter, obtaining descriptively better point estimates whose uncertainty is assessed with paired comparisons. LASR thus provides a principled offline protocol for measuring action-related predictive support in world-model latents.

title: Quantum annealing through a first-order phase transition: Field theory approach
abstract: Unlike second-order phase transitions, a first-order transition has a stage, in which a system is trapped in a metastable state. The decay of this state leads to abundant excitations over the ground state. We present a field theory for kinetics of defects emerging during quantum annealing computations. This theory predicts several power laws for the error generation rate during quantum annealing either though or near the first-order phase transition. Sharp changes between the power exponents are predicted for continuous parameter changes. Observation of this behavior would be a signature of first-order critical points and could help identify and avoid them for better computations. The driven Lipkin-Meshkov-Glick model (LMGm) serves as the minimal model of interacting Ising spins that demonstrates this behavior.

title: Dual-Stage Channel-Posterior Integration for MLM-Aided Token Communications
abstract: Token transmission over conventional digital modulation is vulnerable to channel impairments, leading to bit errors that cause received tokens to become contextually inconsistent. This paper proposes a receiver-side dual-stage channel-posterior integration framework for masked language model (MLM)-aided token reconstruction. In the proposed framework, the receiver detects unreliable token positions from channel reliability and constructs a vocabulary-level channel-posterior. In particular, within the receiver, Posterior-Weighted Input Embedding (PWE) injects this posterior into the MLM input, while Adaptive Output Logit Fusion (AOF) reuses it at the output with a channel-adaptive weight. Consequently, multiple unreliable tokens can be reconstructed in a single bidirectional MLM inference without retransmission, transmitter-side encoding, or additional MLM training. Experiments over noisy channels show up to a $67.2$\% improvement in cosine similarity over context-only MLM reconstruction, with consistent gains across different MLM architectures and existing language-model-aided methods.

title: Clustering-Based Artificial Tree Ensembles for Random Forest Approximation
abstract: Random Forests (RFs) offer strong prediction performance but are difficult to interpret. Most representative trees (MRTs) and artificial representative trees (ARTs) provide surrogate explanations, but a single tree may miss patterns within a forest. We investigate benefits and limitations of clustering-based representative tree ensembles for RF surrogate modeling and assess the contribution of similarity-based clustering relative to random tree partitions. Using linear and nonlinear simulations and regression benchmarks, we evaluate fidelity, prediction accuracy, complexity, and prediction stability against equally sized ensembles of top-ranked MRTs and randomly selected trees. Increasing ensemble size generally improves fidelity, accuracy, and prediction stability. ART ensembles show higher fidelity in simulations and often greater prediction stability for small ensembles. Compared with random tree partitions, similarity-based clustering generally improves ART fidelity in simulations and often on benchmarks. On benchmark datasets, MRT-based ensembles generally achieve higher fidelity and prediction accuracy, whereas ART ensembles have fewer terminal nodes. ART ensembles provide compact surrogates when reduced complexity matters and their fidelity and prediction accuracy meet application requirements. These findings clarify both the trade-offs of representative tree ensembles as RF surrogates and the contribution of similarity-based clustering beyond random clustering.

title: VelServe: Taming Decode Jitters in LLM Inference with Tail-Calibrated Scheduling
abstract: Interactive LLM services must meet latency service-level objectives (SLOs) for the time to first token (TTFT) and the time between tokens (TBT), as streaming and soft real-time applications require predictable token delivery. We identify decode jitters in both aggregated and disaggregated serving. A jitter delays every request in the batch, and long responses span hundreds of steps, so even rare overruns cause many SLO violations. In aggregated serving, SLO-aware schedulers set each step's prefill budget until its predicted latency just meets the TBT target, leaving no room for mispredictions or host stalls. Disaggregation meets average TBT targets at a cost in capacity, yet the steps that admit new requests still run late. We present \sysname, a scheduler that calibrates how much prefill work each decode step carries using the measured tail of its own iteration latency. The SLO determines how rare a late step must be, and \sysname leaves enough headroom in each iteration to prevent overruns and meet the target decode latency. This headroom slows prefill, so \sysname serves the shortest waiting prompt first. When TTFT deadlines grow with prompt length, the long prompts it delays have the most time to spare. Under disaggregation, it spaces admissions so that no request waits on more slow admission steps than its P99 target allows. On three attention families and varying workloads, \sysname sustains 2.4--2.9$\times$ the SLO goodput of the strongest baseline on Qwen3-8B and DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and at least 4.4$\times$ on DeepSeek-V2-Lite. With prefill and decode disaggregated on eight GPUs, \sysname meets the SLO for more than twice as many requests as state-of-the-art baselines.

title: Supercharging Olmo-core for Efficient and Scalable MoE Training
abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models add parameters without proportionally increasing per-token compute. However, training cost also depends on bytes moved, memory held, and kernels launched, and many of those costs follow total parameter size rather than active compute. On infrastructure built for dense models, this mismatch is costly: in early baselines, throughput fell as stored expert parameter size grew, even though the useful work per token stayed nearly fixed. To close this gap, we present a redesigned training stack in Olmo-core, built for efficient, scalable MoE training. We replace the Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) of earlier Olmo-core versions with an architecture built on Distributed Data Parallel (DDP), and add Expert Parallelism (EP), Pipeline Parallelism (PP), a distributed optimizer, and activation recompute. We propose NVSHMEM-based rowwise EP, which writes each token directly into its expert's buffer, avoiding dispatch and combine permutation overhead. We make EP fully synchronization-free by keeping routing metadata on the GPU and using device-scheduled grouped GEMMs. Closely integrated MXFP8 cuts compute, activation-memory, and transport costs, and topology-agnostic checkpoints let the parallel layout change between runs. On NVL8 B300 nodes, the stack supports training configurations from 12.9 billion to 1.2 trillion total parameters on up to 512 GPUs, reaching 858 useful-model TFLOP/s/GPU at 1.2 trillion with MXFP8 and per-layer recompute; an experimental capacity test with the optional DeepEP v2 backend reaches 2.38 trillion. We also explain each design choice and share findings for other training systems; for example, we identify a failure pattern we call Token Gerrymandering, in which the MoE router can learn to hack the load-balancing loss, and find that overlapping communication with computation can slow the overlapped kernels by more than it hides.

title: A systematic comparison of physics-informed neural networks and mechanistic models for epidemic modeling and forecasting
abstract: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have recently been applied to epidemic modeling and forecasting with promising results. These methods integrate mechanistic knowledge with data-driven learning. Yet, their comparative performance against well-established, and simpler epidemic models is underexplored. Here, we conduct a systematic comparison of a PINN-based framework and a stochastic mechanistic model. Both approaches share the same age-structured SEIRD core and rolling-window forecasting pipeline, in a deliberately minimal setting. We evaluate their retrospective fits and probabilistic forecasts in two synthetic scenarios and the first COVID-19 wave in London. Interestingly, while PINNs underperform in synthetic scenarios, they achieve better performance on real data. Furthermore, PINNs provide narrower uncertainty intervals and sharper estimation of parameters in synthetic scenarios. Our findings confirm PINNs as a promising tool in epidemiology. At the same time, the results reaffirm the value of simpler approaches such as traditional compartmental models, and promote additional benchmarking studies.

title: Conflict, Feasibility, Faithfulness, Displacement: Four Quantities That Come Apart in Federated Dual-Cone Aggregation
abstract: FedFV, FedGH and FedMGDA+ aggregate client updates with multi-objective gradient aggregators to remove conflict between them. We examine this rationale with UPGrad, which increases no client's loss to first order, in a comparison that changes only the direction of FedAvg's update. Four quantities the rationale treats as one -- conflict between client updates, feasibility of their weighted mean, faithfulness of the transmitted updates to the clients' gradients, and displacement of the update -- come apart. Under Dirichlet partitioning UPGrad improves CIFAR-10 accuracy by +0.78 pp (14/15 seeds, p < 0.001), only with full participation; on Oxford-IIIT Pet its +0.52 pp gain vanishes (+0.07 pp) once the data our protocol left unused are kept. Varying only the Dirichlet concentration, the gain grows with heterogeneity, yet the split with the most conflict shows none. Uniform client weights, blind to conflict, match the CIFAR-10 gain and exceed the Pets gain; a matched random rotation does neither. No fairness effect survives multiplicity correction, and on CIFAR-10 the guarantee does not reach the clients' gradients. We state what evaluations should report.

Uniform client weights, blind to conflict, match the CIFAR-10 gain and exceed the Pets gain; a matched random rotation does neither. No fairness effect survives multiplicity correction, and on CIFAR-10 the guarantee does not reach the clients' gradients. We state what evaluations should report.

title: Activation Steering the Nan-Shan in Typhoon
abstract: Typhoon is an audiovisual installation based on Joseph Conrad's novella, in which Captain MacWhirr steers the steamer Nan-Shan directly into and through a catastrophic storm. The novella is a study of what happens when the scale of a phenomenon exceeds the practical and conceptual frameworks available to comprehend it and of the paralysis that sometimes follows a demand for action in such overwhelming circumstances. We chose the text of Typhoon to reflect on human culture's current AI moment. We prompt a large language model, seeded with Conrad's original language, to feed endlessly on its own output, and explore when and how the text becomes increasingly alien and unwieldy as time progresses, including deviations from the narrative, digressions into the model's own instructions and thinking, and long periods of incoherent rumination. We employ methods from activation steering, including a novel adaptive steering method we introduce, to control the rhythm of the narrative and the model's digressions over long stretches of generation. The simultaneous efficacy and unpredictability of this steering showcases the tension between the perceived interpretability of AI, and the reality of a system that remains outside our comprehension and control.

title: From Language-Specific to Cross-DSL: Semantic-Role-Guided Model Completion with LLMs
abstract: The rapid emergence of large language models (LLMs), trained on vast and diverse corpora, has positioned them as a promising source of domain knowledge to assist modelers. However, leveraging LLMs for model completion remains challenging: suggestions must respect both the syntax of a domain-specific language (DSL) and the intended domain semantics, while remaining consistent with an evolving model. This paper presents RAFiC, an LLM-based approach for iterative domain model completion that generalizes across DSLs. It drives completion using metamodel information to ensure syntactic validity and enriches prompts with semantic-role annotations to better capture the intended modeling role of DSL elements. The approach provides context-aware, incremental guidance during model construction. We evaluate RAFiC through an ablation-based comparative study over three DSLs and two scenarios per DSL to isolate the contribution of syntactic and semantic guidance. Across these six scenarios, semantic role guidance improves contribution rate in every case, and RAFiC improves completion effectiveness over weaker prompting configurations in most of them. The largest gains occur for DSLs that are less represented in LLM training data. In these cases, iterative guidance leads to earlier and more stable accepted suggestions, while semantic role guidance improves their relevance.

title: Where Tree Ensembles Decide: Structural Local Explanation with Decision Predicate Graphs
abstract: Tree ensembles are among the most accurate models for tabular data, yet the computation behind a single prediction is spread over hundreds of decision rules. Feature attributions and counterfactuals explain such predictions through the influence of features or a change of the input, leaving open which of the thresholds applied by the trees a prediction responds to, while structural explanations compress these rules and lose the trees behind them. To address this gap, we propose a local Decision Predicate Graph (local DPG), which gathers the rules executed for a sample into a verifiable record of the computation, with a class support that reproduces every explained prediction. From these rules we select the critical predicate, the executed predicate whose crossing is estimated to move the model most strongly toward a chosen class, which offers the user a concrete threshold and the trees that share it, without an external explainer. Across 16 datasets and four ensemble families, it separates differently predicted neighbours better than random and nearest-threshold predicates. A single crossing recovers the true class in 46-69% of wrong predictions, against 29-50% when the same rule is applied to the feature ranked first by TreeSHAP, a measure close to the selection criterion, and on planted faults it finds the faulty threshold in 46-71% of the resulting errors, against 6-21% at random. Although training-free edits of these predicates did not reduce the error on unseen data, the critical predicate complements attributions and counterfactuals by naming where a prediction can be changed.

title: Sample-Efficient Control of Magnetoconvective Flows via Differentiable Simulation
abstract: Magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) fluid flows are central to demanding engineering applications, most prominently fusion blanket cooling, where flow control is a promising tool to optimize key properties such as heat transfer. While active flow control (AFC) has recently advanced through machine learning, its application to MHD flows remains largely unexplored. In this work, we present $φ$-PICT, a novel differentiable GPU-accelerated MHD solver targeted at AFC. We validate $φ$-PICT against MHD benchmarks and demonstrate its high computational efficiency. Integrated into FluidGym, $φ$-PICT enables sample-efficient gradient-based algorithms to improve heat transfer by $>25$% and allows optimizers to achieve $10^3\times$ higher accuracy in inverse design than black-box methods. $φ$-PICT is publicly available at https://github.com/upb-sciml/phiPICT.

title: Reasoning More, Knowing No Better? Epistemic Calibration in Financial Reasoning Tasks
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) reportedly 'reason' with increasing sophistication, but whether they 'know' when they are wrong remains poorly understood. We study epistemic calibration, the alignment between expressed confidence and empirical correctness, across approximately 30 contemporary models and configurable reasoning-effort budgets, using XFinBench (graduate-level financial reasoning) and SQuAD v2 (answerable and unanswerable questions). Reported confidence stays high relative to accuracy, with weak discrimination between correct and incorrect or unsupported answers. Miscalibration follows a Dunning-Kruger-like pattern: weaker models are often strongly overconfident, while frontier models are mildly underconfident. Reasoning effort significantly improves accuracy but has no detectable effect on the confidence-accuracy gap or ECE; stable between-model differences explain over 96% of calibration variance, versus a negligible effort effect. Calibration deteriorates most on scenario planning and numerical modeling. On SQuAD v2, models answer four in five unanswerable questions and remain near-maximally confident even when no answer is supported; higher reasoning effort yields no robust gain in calibration or abstention after multiplicity correction. We discuss implications for evaluation, deployment, and the design of calibration-aware, boundary-aware financial reasoning systems.

title: Effects of Conventional, Adaptive, and AI-Powered Upscaling on the Legibility of License Plates
abstract: Small details in digital images -- a face, a street sign, a license plate -- are routinely upscaled in hopes of making them interpretable. Upscaling options now range from conventional interpolation, whose operations are spatially invariant and fully explainable, to AI-powered methods that synthesize detail potentially absent from the source. Here, we ask which of these techniques most reliably helps human readers. In two online experiments, we measured legibility of 255 US license plates ranging in resolution from 128 to 8 pixels tall, as well as their legibility after upscaling by eight different methods. Legibility of the un-upscaled plates collapsed from ceiling to floor across a narrow band of plate heights (32 to 10 pixels). Conventional upscaling techniques (bilinear, bicubic, and Lanczos interpolation) gave modest gains of about 5-9 percentage points within this range. Nearest-neighbor interpolation, however, was harmful, rendering unreadable many plates that were readable without any upscaling. Advanced methods diverged: SwinIR, an open-source AI enhancer, raised performance by up to 38 points relative to no upscaling, while an adaptive denoiser-based image prior and commercial AI upscaler tended to impair legibility. We found no strong evidence of consistent character hallucinations across methods. Decomposing the task, conventional interpolators mainly helped readers count characters, whereas SwinIR alone made the characters themselves more identifiable.

title: Structure makes quantum circuits trainable
abstract: The scalability of variational quantum algorithms is limited by barren plateaus, where gradients vanish exponentially in system size. This worst-case result raises fundamental questions about the trainability of quantum AI models. We present a major advance towards resolving this trainability question by answering whether a given quantum circuit has a barren plateau. We do this using an analytical framework that bounds the gradient variance for arbitrary input states $ρ$ and observables $\mathcal{M}$ by decomposing the unitary representation of the associated compact Lie group. When the circuit segments on both sides of a gate form $2$-designs, we obtain the variance exactly and prove a sufficient condition for trainability: if $ρ^{\otimes 2}$ and $\mathcal{M}^{\otimes 2}$ are sufficiently concentrated on the same irreducible invariant subspace of polynomial dimension, and the differentiated gate moves this subspace by an inverse-polynomial amount, then the gradient variance is at least inverse-polynomial. We further present a sampling algorithm that estimates the gradient variance from runs of the ansatz, without constructing the representation-theoretic projectors. Our algorithm decides whether the variance exceeds a tolerance $τ$ with the number of runs polynomial in $1/τ$, including cases in which the bounds are inconclusive. This resolves the question of the trainability of the circuit before expensive training procedures.

title: RecurIR: Learning When and How to Revise Restoration Policies via Recursive Self-Improvement
abstract: Agent-based image restoration has achieved promising performance by coordinating restoration tools to handle heterogeneous and coupled degradations. However, existing agents often improve their decisions through accumulated successful and failed executions, without explicitly identifying the conditions under which learned restoration strategies remain effective. Consequently, changes in degradation severity, spatial coverage, or interactions may invalidate previous decisions, while providing limited guidance on how these decisions should be revised. In this paper, we propose \textbf{RecurIR}, a recursive self-improvement framework that enables restoration agents to learn when and how to revise their decision rules. Specifically, we introduce a policy-hypothesis discovery mechanism to identify testable, condition-dependent rules through matched tool executions. We then design a rule-falsification-driven task evolution mechanism to generate targeted degradation variations, examine the validity of learned rules, and identify their applicability boundaries. Based on the resulting evidence, we develop a change-conditioned policy revision mechanism that learns how variations in degradation conditions should modify tool selection, execution order, operation strength, and processing regions. We further incorporate independent verification to retain effective revisions and use the resulting feedback to guide subsequent hypothesis discovery and task evolution. Through this recursive process, RecurIR progressively refines its restoration policies as degradation conditions change. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework.

title: GDP.xlsx: Benchmarking Frontier Models on Professional Workbooks
abstract: We introduce GDP_xlsx, a benchmark of 70 realistic workplace requests written by professionals in 13 domains, each paired with an expert rubric of binary criteria and with the complete workbook or CSV file it refers to. Together the files hold 2.18 million populated cells, and the rubrics 791 criteria. Agents work in a container with spreadsheet tools, and an agentic judge that can open the file applies the rubric. Completeness and exclusivity criteria require set-valued answers to be found in full and with nothing extra. We rank models by strict pass@1, the share of attempts that meet every criterion. Across 20 model configurations, including frontier models from Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI, the top-scoring one, Gemini 4 Argon, passes only 38.3% of attempts, and the median score is 19.3%, leaving wide headroom. We release the evaluation harness and three public tasks; the other 67 are held out to protect the leaderboard from contamination.

title: When Does Cross-View Consistency Matter in Multi-View Appearance Augmentation? A Controlled Study for Visuomotor Policies
abstract: Multi-view visual augmentation often seeks consistency across cameras, but it is unclear which forms of consistency matter for downstream control. We use simulation-state replay to manipulate cross-view coupling while preserving the per-camera perturbation distributions, physical trajectories, and action labels. Across seven LIBERO manipulation tasks, marginal-matched changes in global appearance, ghost injection, and target color have small average costs for a late-fusion Diffusion Policy: point estimates are near zero or negative, and the largest upper endpoint of the 90% posterior credible intervals is 2.55 percentage points. In contrast, geometrically anti-coupled observations reduce success by 3.30 percentage points relative to coupled observations (90% CrI [0.64, 6.28]), with displacement magnitude, direction marginals, and the number of affected views matched. Camera interventions reveal substantial dependence on wrist-view geometry, while feature analysis shows appearance sensitivity patterns associated with the factors randomized during training. ACT shows a higher target-color cost estimate than DP, with uncertainty that includes zero and sensitivity to task composition. Within the tested tasks and policy configurations, these findings motivate selective consistency constraints: appearance coupling can sometimes be relaxed, whereas task-relevant geometry and cross-view spatial correspondence warrant protection.

title: Between the Lines: Multi-turn Contextual Investment Advice Detection
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) increasingly power financial conversational assistants, detecting investment advice in natural language has become a critical regulatory and safety challenge. Unlike explicit single-turn recommendations, investment advice often emerges implicitly and progressively over multi-turn conversations, shaped by user intent, delivery style, and contextual buildup. We introduce the first comprehensive framework for detecting both sequential and contextual investment advice in dialogue settings. Central to our approach is a modular, top-down synthetic data generation pipeline that systematically spans a taxonomy of advisory trajectories using an axis-bucket-descriptor schema. We simulate both benign and high-risk conversations across diverse user personas, financial instruments, and risk tiers, and evaluate detection capabilities using LLM-as-a-Judge with entropy-based uncertainty diagnostics. Our results show that contextual advisory detection remains substantially more challenging than sequential cases, even under few-shot prompting with tailored demonstrations. This work lays the foundation for scalable guardrail development in highstakes, compliance-sensitive domains, where advisory risk is often subtle, distributed, and perception-dependent.

title: Learned Regularization for Sparse-View CT: Accuracy, Lesion Detectability and Distribution Shift of a Plug-and-Play Prior against Tuned Total Variation
abstract: Learned image priors are often proposed to replace hand-crafted regularizers in sparse-view computed tomography (CT), yet they are usually judged by PSNR on data resembling their training set. We evaluate one noise-conditioned DnCNN denoiser used as a Plug-and-Play prior against filtered back-projection (FBP), Tikhonov and total-variation (TV) regularization, with every method tuned on validation data and all differences paired. On synthetic 28x28 digit images, the prior beats box-constrained TV by about 3.4 dB at moderate noise (sigma = 0.05, 20 angles), but the advantage shrinks at low noise and reverses under distribution shift: an MNIST-trained prior is 3.1 dB (Fashion-MNIST) and 4.3-4.6 dB (Shepp-Logan phantom) below TV, whereas a Fashion-MNIST-trained prior beats TV by 2.2 dB on Fashion-MNIST, consistent with prior mismatch rather than a failure of PnP itself. In a lesion-insertion test the prior detects lesions worse than TV in distribution despite its higher PSNR, and under mismatch it produces more lesion-like false blobs than box-constrained TV for seven of eight lesion types. On real LoDoPaB-CT slices (patient-disjoint split; 30, 60 and 120 angles; three dose levels; 40 test patients), the prior does not consistently outperform a well-tuned TV in PSNR (-0.93 to +0.33 dB) and has lower SSIM in eight of nine conditions. Its lesion-detection AUC is higher than this TV's in all nine conditions (significant in six) but never significantly higher than that of Hann-filtered FBP, which the PSNR-tuned TV falls below in detection in all nine conditions (seven significant). On non-anatomical phantoms its PSNR falls below TV in all six conditions. PSNR and lesion detectability thus rank the methods differently. Our conclusions concern one small denoiser, and the CT analysis was developed after seeing results, without pre-specified primary comparisons.
